question: Why did the 1988 Japanese Canadian Redress Agreement involve more than a symbolic federal apology?
generated_answer: The 1988 Japanese Canadian Redress Agreement was more than a symbolic apology because it included a $21,000 payment to each surviving individual who was interned or whose property was confiscated during World War II. Additionally, the agreement provided for the creation of a community fund to support Japanese Canadian heritage and education initiatives. This financial compensation and community support were essential components of the agreement, demonstrating a commitment to addressing the material and social impacts of the internment on Japanese Canadians. The agreement also recognized the injustices of the past and acknowledged the role of the Canadian government in perpetuating those injustices, which was a crucial step towards reconciliation. Overall, the 1988 Japanese Canadian Redress Agreement was a comprehensive effort to address the historical wrongs committed against Japanese Canadians, and its inclusion of financial compensation and community support made it more than just a symbolic apology.
